Triggers.value: Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath
Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
Medical equipment such as needles or drips

Maladaptive Strategies.value: control eating strictly to feel in control

Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

issues.item: Triggers: Victim Memories: Reminders of victims
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'Reminders of victims' is hard to reconcile with the trauma type; it implies exposure to other victims in a disaster/assault context rather than illness-related trauma.

'Being naked' as a trigger is difficult to connect to life-threatening illness unless there is a very specific medical context; with the other selected items it appears context-incongruent rather than illness-linked.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction
issues.explanation: Rehearsing conversations before any interaction suggests prominent social-evaluative anxiety, but there are no corresponding appraisal or threat items about humiliation, criticism, or social danger; this strategy is poorly matched to the rest of the profile.

'Being naked' is a poor fit as a primary trigger for a life-threatening illness profile unless the illness/trauma specifically involved exposure or bodily vulnerability in that context; with the rest of this profile centered on somatic and medical cues, this item stands out as clinically incoherent.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction
issues.explanation: Rehearsing conversations before any interaction suggests prominent social-evaluative anxiety or interpersonal threat management, which is not supported by the other selected trigger, memory, appraisal, or threat items and does not fit the stated illness-centered formulation.

issues.item: Threat: Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
issues.explanation: Always choosing a safe/protected seat implies environmental danger monitoring more typical of assault/combat/public threat trauma than life-threatening illness; it is weakly connected to the medical/somatic trigger pattern here.

issues.item: Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
issues.explanation: For a 37-year-old man with trauma centered on a life-threatening illness, the threat profile is otherwise strongly somatic/medical (negative emotions, body on alert) and the trigger/strategy pattern is specifically tied to breathlessness, procedures, and medical cues. A prominent exaggerated startle to ordinary sounds is not impossible, but in this profile it appears disconnected from the illness-related trigger network and from the cognitive formulation, where Threat is mainly linked with Maladaptive Strategies rather than a broad sensory hypervigilance pattern. This makes the item clinically incoherent relative to the rest of the selected items.

vignette: Ethan, a 37‑year‑old database administrator from a small town in the Midwest, had always been the steady, quiet type—accurate with his code, meticulous about his meals, and comfortable in the predictability of his work schedule. When he was taken to the emergency department after a sudden collapse, the routine was shattered. He had never before felt so suddenly vulnerable; the bright fluorescent lights of the triage room, the sharp hiss of the oxygen tubing, and the stinging feel of the IV needle as the nurse inserted it were all the more vivid against the backdrop of his fear. The doctors told him he had suffered a massive pulmonary embolism, that a clot had traveled from his leg to his lungs and had nearly ended his life. He was intubated, sedated, and placed on a ventilator for days. The memory of that moment—hands gripping his chest, the taste of antiseptic, the cold metal of the breathing tube—remained as clear and terrifying as if it had happened yesterday. The threat he sensed from that event did not disappear when the tube was removed. Instead, it settled into the muscle of his body, an almost constant tension that made him feel that danger could return at any instant. In the weeks that followed, Ethan noticed that even simple thoughts of “breathing” or “medical procedures” triggered a fluttering in his chest and a racing heart. The threat of a sudden medical crisis had become part of his everyday experience. Because of that persistent sense of threat, he began to adopt a strict eating schedule, believing that controlling his calorie intake would give him a semblance of control over his body’s unpredictable response. The more he restricted his food, the more he felt that his body was constantly on edge, and the fear of the next crisis seemed to grow in tandem with his hunger. This belief—his threat had made him feel that any deviation from control could provoke a life‑threatening event—became the foundation for his maladaptive strategies. His avoidance patterns multiplied. After the ICU stay, the thought of stepping outside for a walk became unbearable. The very idea of exercise was associated with the feeling of breathlessness he had experienced in the hospital; the fear that his heart might surge and he would need to be rushed to the ER again. So he stopped jogging, skipping his morning walks, and even declined to walk with his sister to a grocery store. The avoidance of physical activity not only removed a healthy outlet but also reinforced the body’s sense that it was fragile and unsteady. When he finally did a short stroll around the block, his lungs seemed to protest, his chest tightened, and his breathing felt labored. That experience amplified his threat perception, feeding back into the belief that exercise was dangerous. The avoidance thus kept the loop of threat and fear alive. Ethan also became increasingly cautious about any medical cue. The mere sight of a white coat or the sound of a stethoscope could send a wave of panic through him. The avoidance of hospitals and clinics meant that routine health checks were postponed; his routine blood work and minor vaccinations fell through the cracks. In the workplace, his careful attention to detail made him double‑check everything, but when he accidentally left a database field blank, he would panic, feeling as if the error could cause a catastrophic system failure. The fear of being caught, the anticipation of a negative reaction from colleagues, and the threat of a personal health crisis all converged in this moment, causing his body to shiver, his heart to race, and his thoughts to spiral. This cascade of threat, maladaptive strategy, and trigger solidified the cycle. For months, Ethan’s avoidance and threat perceptions grew. His relationship with his ex‑wife deteriorated because he would not leave the house to meet her, fearing that a health crisis might occur while she was there, and she could be left in a dangerous situation. At work, he missed a critical system upgrade because the prospect of a brief emergency assessment by an IT specialist made him feel that he was inviting a crisis. He found himself constantly scanning his environment for any hint of medical equipment, and his diet had become so restrictive that he began to experience dizziness, which in turn made his breathing feel even more labored. The feedback loop of threat, avoidance, and maladaptive strategy had become a self‑reinforcing spiral. The tipping point came when, during a routine meeting, Ethan felt a tightness in his chest that escalated into a full panic attack. He left the room abruptly, the alarm in his chest growing louder than the voice of his manager. That night, he could not sleep, replaying in his mind the image of the hospital bed, the needle, and the cold, white walls. He realized that his life had become a series of controlled actions and avoided moments, and that he had been living in constant hypervigilance. It was then that he reached out to a therapist, hoping to untangle the web of fear that bound him to his own body. He is most afraid that his avoidance will continue to erode his health and relationships, yet he also holds a quiet hope that, with guidance, he can regain agency over his breathing and his life.
